results.title: Origins and Application of the Translation Theorem in Extremely Low Lunar Orbits
results.abstract: Extremely low lunar orbits (eLLOs) (altitudes ?≤50??km) are highly perturbed by the nonspherical lunar gravitational field, presenting unique challenges to orbit maintenance. At these altitudes, stable ?frozen? orbits do not exist, and conventional station-keeping methods such as circularization tend to be ineffective. However, a distinctive dynamic feature has been observed in such orbits, dubbed the ?translation theorem,? wherein the eccentricity vector follows a predictable monthly evolution that is largely independent of initial conditions. In this work, the dynamic origins of this effect are identified; it results from a combination of low orbital eccentricity with the dominant effects of a particular subset of sectoral and tesseral harmonics. Based on this result, automated station-keeping strategies for eLLOs are developed, which leverage eccentricity vector control. Several constraints for station-keeping within the eccentricity vector plane are explored, including circular, annular, and elevation-model-derived regions, each forming distinct strategies for varying orbital configurations. The optimal control profiles for these strategies in the ephemeris model are then obtained using sequential convex programming (SCP). These station-keeping strategies offer computational simplicity while achieving ?v costs that are comparable to full trajectory optimization.

results.title: Small Satellite Hybrid Propulsion Systems: A Numerical Strategy for Regenerative Cooling Design
results.abstract: With the rise of green propulsion systems alongside the growing need for an easier access to space by private aerospace companies and small satellite research groups, hybrid rocket engines start representing an attractive option for in-space propulsion because of their inherent advantages, such as safety, low toxicity, and low cost. However, challenges emerge in case of miniaturized engines requiring long-duration firings and/or multiple ignitions (as foreseen in different small satellite applications), since ablative passive thermal protection systems typically employed in the nozzle suffer excessive throat erosion and general thermal management issues. To address this, the present study proposes an efficient numerical approach for designing and analyze active regenerative cooling systems for small satellite hybrid propulsion, using carbon-based nozzles and liquid nitrous oxide (i.e., N2O) as coolant. The mathematical model proposed is firstly validated using data of an actively-cooled hybrid engine prototype recently tested at the Hokkaido University. The phase-change behavior of N2O is looked in details, and an evaporation rate law is proposed based on an ad-hoc reconstruction technique. Then, a simplified cooling system scalability study is carried out, underlining the potential advantages of a graphite-based liner over classical metal-based cooling jackets configurations. Lastly, an optimization algorithm for parametric design and optimization of the cooling system is introduced. The design algorithm is used to analyze two thrust-classes (≈100N and ≈1N) representative of hybrid engines in development at Letara Ltd., revealing that, while designing efficient cooling systems becomes more challenging with smaller engine scales, both engine scales can be successfully cooled using regenerative cooling methods, even considering manufacturing constraints related to 3D printing limits.

results.title: A Model-Based Tool for Anomaly Management
results.abstract: MAGE formalizes a largely informal and experience-led decision-making process in small satellite anomaly management. It is especially useful when only limited telemetry data is available or novice groups of engineers, such as small-satellite university programs, encounter anomalies. These groups tend to be resource constrained in schedule, budget, and expertise. By leveraging hybrid model-based methods and logical reasoning, MAGE provides a structured, formalized, high-level approach to fault detection, diagnosis, and resolution that can be navigated effectively by novice and experienced operators. This comprehensive method extends beyond traditional fault trees, addressing the limitations posed by incomplete information and the potential biases of past experiences. The classification of anomalies is especially useful for understanding and resolving them. An existing spacecraft mission was used to validate MAGE. The results of which illustrate the practical application and benefits of MAGE, showcasing its ability to work with abstract models and limited data. Thus, this tool enables novice teams to manage spacecraft anomalies and potentially save their missions from failure. The versatility of MAGE and its integration of operator intent further enhance its utility, making it a valuable tool to ensure the success and reliability of future space missions.

results.title: Sliding Mode Control With Chattering Reduction
results.abstract: Sliding Mode Control is a powerful nonlinear control methodology that can handle parametric uncertainties and external disturbances. However, the discontinuous and high-frequency switching nature of the control law introduces the chattering phenomenon, which leads to potential actuator degradation, alterations to the desired response characteristics and, sometimes, instability during control implementation. The main objective of this paper is to study Sliding Mode Control with chattering reduction. The Sliding Mode Control law involves an equivalent control component and a discontinuous control component. A disturbance estimation is performed based on Lyapunov analysis and adaptive control techniques and then included in the Sliding Mode Control law as part of the equivalent control term. As a result, the Sliding Mode Control gain could be set to a smaller constant value so as to reduce chattering. The modified controller is tested on a simulation model of the rotational dynamics of a small satellite experiencing constant disturbances using quaternion kinematics and Euler?s equations of rotational motion. Furthermore, a Conventional Sliding Mode Controller and an Adaptive Controller are also designed using Lyapunov analysis. The error quaternion and angular velocities are driven towards the identity quaternion and zero respectively using all three control methods and a comparative analysis of the results obtained is conducted.

results.title: A Hosted Payload Cyber Attack Against Satellites
results.abstract: The increased utilization of small satellites, particularly CubeSats, has been propelled by technological advancements and the widespread incorporation of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) components. This transition has ushered in a paradigm of faster and more cost- effective missions, giving rise to novel trends such as the Internet of Space Things (IoST) and Space as a Service (SaaS) in the space domain. However, this shift comes with a concomitant rise in spacecraft architecture complexity, expanding the attack surface for potential cyber threats. Despite these advancements, space cybersecurity has lagged behind, largely adhering to traditional security-through-obscurity approaches, thereby endangering the security of future missions and critical infrastructure. This work delves into the OPS-SAT mission as a case study, presenting one of the most advanced CubeSat missions to date. OPS-SAT introduces innovative mission capabilities and novel concepts in space operations. In this study, we assume the role of malicious users, crafting and executing a cyber attack against the primary payload of the OPS-SAT spacecraft, within an emulated environment. The success of the attack is scrutinized, and the resultant impacts across the system are systematically enumerated. The study culminates in a formalized representation of the attack using established threat modeling frameworks, including attack trees and the SPARTA matrix. This approach offers a comprehensive examination of the OPS-SAT mission?s susceptibility to cyber threats, providing insights that can inform future cybersecurity strategies for advanced small satellite missions.

results.title: Wildfire Identification Via CMOS Sensor Fitted High-Altitude Long Endurance (HALE) System
results.abstract: Abstract Wildfires cause millions of dollars of damage each year and affect countless lives and habitats. Because of this, wildfire monitoring techniques have become necessary to protect property and natural ecosystems. Advances in Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) have allowed for safer, more cost-effective monitoring systems of forest fires. A constellation of high-altitude long-endurance (HALE) fixed-wing aircraft, such as the Airbus Zephyr S, with a camera system designed to detect forest fires, could be used to monitor high-risk wildfire areas constantly. The challenges of wildfire surveillance, such as aircraft type, altitude, search patterns, number of aircraft, and wind speed are reviewed to create a concept of operations for using a HALE UAS to detect wildfires. Additionally, a camera system capable of detecting wavelengths of light emitted by burning potassium in plant matter will be analyzed as a possible solution to current multispectral sensor system challenges when attempting to detect wildfire sources. A proof of concept of this system has been designed. Likewise, an apparatus designed to test a prototype version of this camera system has been created.

results.title: Extended Lifetime of CubeSats in the Lower Thermosphere with Active Attitude Control
results.abstract: A wide variety of missions could be enabled by extended orbital flight in extreme low Earth orbit, defined as an altitude range of 150?250 km. This study investigates the feasibility of a nanosatellite (mass <10??kg) using a propulsive, attitude control system in conjunction with a primary propulsion system to extend mission life. The primary propulsion system consists of a pair of electrospray thrusters providing a combined thrust of 0.12 mN at 1 W. Pulsed plasma thrusters are used for attitude control. The mission consists of two phases. In Phase I, a 4U CubeSat is deployed from a 414 km orbit and uses the primary propulsion system to deorbit to an initial altitude within the targeted range of 244±10??km. Phase I lasts 12.73 days, with the propulsion system consuming 5.6 g of propellant to deliver a ?V of 28.12 m/s. In Phase II the mission is maintained until the remaining 25.2 g of propellant is consumed. Phase II lasts for 30.27 days, corresponding to a ?V of 57.22 m/s with a mean altitude of 244 km. Using this approach, a primary mission life of 30.27 days could be achieved, compared with 3.1 days without primary propulsion.

results.title: Micropulsed Plasma Thrusters for Attitude Control of a Low-Earth-Orbiting CubeSat
results.abstract: This study presents a 3-Unit CubeSat design with commercial-off-the-shelf hardware, Teflon?-fueled micropulsed plasma thrusters, and an attitude determination and control approach. The micropulsed plasma thruster is sized by the impulse bit and pulse frequency required for continuous compensation of expected maximum disturbance torques at altitudes between 400 and 1000 km, as well as to perform stabilization of up to 20??deg/s and slew maneuvers of up to 180 deg. The study involves realistic power constraints anticipated on the 3-Unit CubeSat. Attitude estimation is implemented using the q method for static attitude determination of the quaternion using pairs of the spacecraft?sun and magnetic-field vectors. The quaternion estimate and the gyroscope measurements are used with an extended Kalman filter to obtain the attitude estimates. Proportional?derivative control algorithms use the static attitude estimates in order to calculate the torque required to compensate for the disturbance torques and to achieve specified stabilization and slewing maneuvers or combinations. The controller includes a thruster-allocation method, which determines the optimal utilization of the available thrusters and introduces redundancy in case of failure. Simulation results are presented for a 3-Unit CubeSat under detumbling, pointing, and pointing and spinning scenarios, as well as comparisons between the thruster-allocation and the paired-firing methods under thruster failure.
